title: Goethe and Schiller Become Friends
text:
For years Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and Friedrich Schiller lived near each other in the small German duchy of Weimar and kept their distance. Goethe was the older, established poet, and Schiller resented his coolness. Their temperaments seemed opposite: Goethe trusted observation and nature, Schiller ideas and philosophy.

In July 1794, after a meeting of a natural science society in Jena, the two happened to leave together and fell into conversation. Goethe described his theory of the metamorphosis of plants and sketched a symbolic primal plant. Schiller listened and shook his head: that was not an experience, he said, but an idea. Goethe recalled being irritated, but the argument drew them together. A few weeks later Schiller wrote him a letter analyzing the nature of Goethe's mind with such insight that Goethe was won over.

For the next ten years they exchanged around a thousand letters, read each other's work, wrote satirical verses together and pushed each other forward. Schiller urged Goethe to return to Faust; Goethe encouraged Schiller's great plays, including Wallenstein and William Tell. When Schiller died in May 1805, Goethe wrote that he had lost a friend and with him half of his own existence.
lesson: Someone very different from you can become your best collaborator. Honest disagreement, taken seriously, can turn into mutual respect that makes both of you better.
people: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Friedrich Schiller
source: Goethe-Schiller correspondence (1794 to 1805); Goethe, "Gluckliches Ereignis" (A Fortunate Encounter, 1817)
